name: Ensulizole
lead: Ensulizole, also known as phenylbenzimidazole sulfonic acid (PBSA) and 2-phenylbenzimidazole-5-sulfonic acid, is a water-soluble organic ultraviolet (UV) filter used in sunscreens and daily facial moisturisers. It is primarily a UVB absorber with minimal UVA coverage, so it is generally combined with other filters when broad-spectrum protection is intended.[1]

Its water solubility, achieved by using the compound as a neutralised salt, lets formulators add it to the water phase of lotions and gels, which proponents of light, non-greasy sunscreens cite as its main attraction.[1] In the United States it is a monograph (over-the-counter) sunscreen active, and its name has appeared on US sunscreen labels since 1999.[1][2]

Published human research on ensulizole specifically is sparse. Most literature concerns sunscreens as a class, photoallergy surveys, in vitro efficacy comparisons and environmental detection in water; none of it tests ensulizole as a looksmaxxing or cosmetic-appearance intervention.

paras: Ensulizole is used in sunscreens, moisturisers with SPF and cosmetics as a UVB absorber. It absorbs mainly in the UVB range (280-315 nm), and in the United States it is typically paired with avobenzone, bemotrizinol, titanium dioxide or zinc oxide for UVA coverage.[1] Outside the US it may be combined with UVA filters such as ecamsule or bisoctrizole.[1]
US drug labels list it alongside other actives, for example with octisalate and zinc oxide in a body sunscreen whose label states it helps prevent sunburn.[2]

An in vitro comparison of 18 EU-authorised filters at their maximum permitted concentrations ranked filters by the sun protection factor they produced in a topical product; it is one of the few comparative datasets that includes this class of filter.[3] A 2012 laboratory study reported that a range of UV filters showed anti-inflammatory effects in addition to absorbing UV.[4]
A registered Phase 3 trial (n=10, 2009) evaluated the sun protection of sunscreen formulas, though the registry entry alone does not establish effect sizes for ensulizole.[5]

Sunscreen chemicals as a group are recognised causes of allergic and photoallergic contact dermatitis. A 15-year clinic review found that 20% of 402 patients with suspected photosensitivity reacted to one or more UV absorbers, and a Swedish series found 7.9% of 355 patients had allergic reactions to tested sunscreen allergens; in both, benzophenone-3 and dibenzoylmethanes figured more prominently than benzimidazoles.[6][7]
US labelling for products containing ensulizole advises external use only, avoiding broken skin, keeping out of eyes, and stopping use if irritation or rash occurs.[2]

Because it is water-soluble and used widely, PBSA is detected in wastewater and surface water, and appears in studies of sorption to sewage sludge.[8][9] In a chronic toxicity test on rainbow trout, researchers examined effects of PBSA after measuring UV filter occurrence in surface water.[10] A 2021 study used biomarkers to assess sublethal effects of ensulizole and octocrylene in the marine mussel Mytilus edulis.[11]

Wikipedia lists ensulizole among sunscreening agents approved by one or more agencies, including the US FDA, the EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety and Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration.[1]

No clinical trial has examined ensulizole on its own for a cosmetic or appearance outcome. The only registered human study found is a small Phase 3 sun-protection formulation test.[5] Broader human data come from photopatch-testing series of sunscreen allergens as a group.[6][7]

timeline.event: The US FDA required the name ensulizole to appear on US sunscreen labels.[1]

card.summary: A water-soluble UVB sunscreen filter for light facial lotions; evidence is sunscreen-class, not appearance-specific.
card.note: Mainly UVB; needs other filters for UVA coverage.

quick.overview:
Ensulizole is an organic sunscreen filter that absorbs mostly UVB light. Because it dissolves in water, it appears in light lotions and daily facial moisturisers with SPF.

It is an approved US over-the-counter sunscreen active. Published research on ensulizole alone is thin; most of what exists covers sunscreen ingredients generally.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVB radiation in the skin-surface layer of a product. It offers little UVA protection, so it is usually combined with filters such as avobenzone, zinc oxide or bemotrizinol.
quick.risks: Sunscreen filters as a group can cause allergic or photoallergic reactions in some people, and labels advise stopping use if rash or irritation occurs. Environmental studies have detected PBSA in water and examined effects on fish and mussels.
